analytic.title: Synthesizing Multirate Programs from IEC 61499

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: IEC 61499 is a standard for designing industrial control systems using function blocks. Since its publication in 2005, several run-time environments have been developed as plausible implementations. Most of them, however, are poorly suited for use in safety-critical systems, as they are unable to guarantee deterministic behaviour and predictable timing. The use of different run-time environments results in subtle behavioural differences and complicates the effort of static timing analysis. We offer an alternative solution by leveraging the model-based approach to automatically synthesize multirate synchronous programs for a multitasking environment. Our approach preserves the well-known deterministic property of synchronous programs, while facilitating static timing analysis of IEC 61499 specifications. We achieve this without the need to introduce any foreign artefact to the standard. The schedulability criterion for tasks derived using our technique is given for the rate-monotonic scheduling policy. The viability of our approach is demonstrated through a code generator, which synthesizes multirate synchronous code for multi-task execution on the μC/OS-II real-time operating system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Model-based design [1] is increasingly touted as a methodology of choice for developing embedded software. The basic idea of this methodology is to use models throughout the development cycle. The high-levels of abstraction afforded by a model-based approach allows a designer to focus on essential functionality, while hiding the tedious implementation details. Model-based approaches generally assume "ideal" semantics, such as concurrent, atomic-step executions of an unlimited number of components [2].

Recognizing these benefits, design tool vendors have begun offering various solutions, such as SIMULINK/STATEFLOW [3] and SCADE [4]. These tools have been successfully used in a variety of safety-critical embedded applications. More recently, model-based design has also been advocated as the new way to develop industrial automation software. The IEC 61499 standard [5] offers an open, vendor-independent modelbased approach for designing industrial control systems. It enables software to be developed in a hierarchical manner using function blocks.

Implementations of IEC 61499 specifications typically involve the use of some run-time environment (e.g., FBRT [6] and FORTE [7]) to enable function block scheduling and event dispatching. These run-time environments have different semantics and temporal properties, which make it difficult to ensure the behavioural consistency and execution times of applications [8]. Such shortcomings need to be addressed in order for IEC 61499 to be used in the design of real-time and safety-critical embedded systems.

In the past, we have proposed the synchronous approach [9] as an alternative way to implement IEC 61499 applications [10]. The synchronous approach was advocated, as it provides ideal temporal primitives to elegantly address the issues of behavioural determinism and temporal predictability. In this idealized model, time is treated as a sequence of discrete instants with nothing happening between the completion of the current instant and the start of the next. All reactions, or computations in response to an input set, complete instantaneously within an instant of time. This is the central tenet of the synchronous approach, and is known as the synchrony hypothesis. The notion of concurrency can, hence, be taken in its most literal sense-events either occur in exactly the same instant (concurrently at the same time), or in distinctly different instants. This ensures behavioural determinism by removing random interleaving between the concurrent parts of a program. Moreover, the requirement that reactions complete within a discrete instant of time imposes a well-defined upper bound to a program's reaction time. This lends itself naturally to the temporal predictability of a program.

The synchrony hypothesis must, of course, be reconciled in the final implementation. Techniques for generating executable code that preserves the semantics of synchronous programs have been extensively studied in literature [9], [11], [12]. Most of these techniques result in a sequential single-task program that is to be executed periodically at a predetermined clock rate. As long as the maximum arrival rate of input events is less than the clock rate, the ideal notion of instantaneous reactions is preserved. However, for programs that consist of concurrent parts with vastly different execution rates, the solution that yields a single task driven by a global clock is not ideal. Programs of this nature are typically referred to as multirate concurrent systems.

Our goal in this paper is, thus, twofold: On one hand, we propose an alternative approach for implementing IEC 61499 specifications, which avoids semantic ambiguity and temporal uncertainty due to the use of run-time environments; on the other hand, we provide a means to specify multirate synchronous programs using the model-based approach of an open standard, from which, multitasking code may be automatically derived. Our contributions are, thus, as follows:

1) We present a technique to realize multirate synchronous programs in a semantic-preserving multitask implementation. Modules of a synchronous program that execute at different rates are modelled as a set of periodic tasks driven by different clocks. The synchrony hypothesis is captured in this model, as each task computes its reaction within a logical time unit of the clock domain it belongs to. 2) We give the schedulability criterion for tasks obtained by applying our technique under the rate-monotonic scheduling (RMS) policy [13]. 3) We present a code generator that synthesizes multitasking code from IEC 61499 descriptions for the μC/OS-II real-time operating system (RTOS) [14].
Communication between tasks running at different rates are implemented as IEC 61499 communication function blocks, with no need for any new artefact to be introduced to the standard.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II provides some brief information on IEC 61499 design artefacts through an example. Section III describes our mapping of IEC 61499 artefacts to multirate synchronous programs, as well as our philosophy for achieving time-predictable systems with this approach. Communication issues for tasks running at different rates are discussed in Section IV. The implementation of our code generator is given in Section V. Finally, we survey some related work in Section VI, before concluding in Section VII.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARIES
div.p: We give a flavour of model-based design with IEC 61499 using a cruise control and monitoring system example adapted from [15]. The main components of this system can be divided into tasks with the following functionality:

• ShaftTask computes the current speed and the cumulative distance according to the rotations of the drive shaft. The current speed is passed to UITask and ControllerTask, while the distance value is sent to InfoTask.
• UITask manages the user inputs from the buttons of the cruise control system and updates the desired cruise speed. This cruise speed is then passed to ControllerTask.
• ControllerTask computes the cruise control state and the throttle output based on the current speed, the desired cruise speed, as well as the brake and accelerator pedal positions.
• InfoTask computes and displays the average speed and fuel consumption since the start of a given trip.

Each task is specified as a distinct resource in IEC 61499. A resource in IEC 61499 is an independent unit of software with its own execution schedule. The behaviour of each resource is itself specified by a network of function blocks, as exemplified in Fig. 1 for the ShaftTask and ControllerTask resources, respectively. IEC 61499 defines three different kinds of function blocks: the basic, composite, and service interface function blocks. They have well-defined input/output interfaces that consist of event and data ports. Event ports are drawn on the upper half of the block, while data ports are drawn on the lower half.

The behaviour of basic function blocks is described by a Moore-type state machine, known as an execution control chart (ECC). On the other hand, the behaviour of composite function blocks is described using a network of function blocks instead of an ECC. This enables the behaviour of a composite block to be hierarchically refined by networks of other blocks. The service interface function block, meanwhile, provides a means to encapsulate platform-specific code (e.g., device drivers) within a function block. All function blocks adopt an event-driven model of execution. A function block is activated whenever it receives an event, which, in turn, may result in the emission of further events that activate other function blocks.

In Fig. 1, some of the service interface function blocks, e.g., those that provide sensor readings (labelled "from SIFB") and actuation (labelled "to SIFB"), have been omitted for brevity. The main functionality of ShaftTask (Fig. 1(a)) is provided by the speedDistSensor function block. It computes the current speed and the cumulative distance travelled based on the shaft rotations of the vehicle. Meanwhile, the controller function block performs the main functionality of ControllerTask (Fig. 1(b)) by computing the cruise control state and throttle output. The monitor function block facilitates this by ensuring that the accelerator pedal is not pressed beyond pedalMin (3 percent), and that the current vehicle speed is within speedMin (30km/h) and speedMax (150km/h).

The controller block also receives events and data from the desiredSpeed and actualSpeed blocks. These two blocks are specialized service interface blocks, known as communication function blocks. In IEC 61499, communication function blocks provide a means for resources to communicate with each other. In Fig. 1, the dotted arrow shows the communication of the speed output from the speedDistSensor block in ShaftTask to ControllerTask via the actualSpeed block of type SEND-uCOS 1. In ControllerTask, this speed value is received by the actualSpeed block of type RECVuCOS 1 and relayed to both the controller and monitor blocks.

div.head: III. REAL-TIME AND SYNCHRONY
div.p: In real-time systems, there are two time lines that are of interest [16]. The first is environment time, which specifies the timing requirements for the interaction of the software program with its physical environment (e.g., sensors, actuators, and clocks), while the second is platform time, which specifies the time needed by the software program to perform a particular operation on a given hardware and RTOS.

In practice, application requirements are typically given in terms of timing constraints for the environment, rather than for the platform. To implement such systems, the programmer is mostly concerned with the relative speeds of the interacting components (e.g., the rate at which events are produced and consumed), rather than with the absolute speeds of execution. Unfortunately, current industrial practice often forces the programmer to reason about timing constraints in terms of platform time. Absolute execution speeds are manipulated through low-level constructs, such as task priorities. Then, for a given priority assignment, the programmer must determine that the scheduling policy and the execution time on the chosen platform will satisfy the timing constraints. This is usually a tedious process, which often results in brittle code.

The synchronous approach takes a different stance to realtime programming by making use of the notion of logical execution time. This ties the execution time of a program to the model, rather than to the platform. Computations are treated as instantaneous reactions to environment inputs, thereby allowing the speeds of different components to be specified relative to an imaginary clock. This removes the tedium of writing precise low-level details for task deadlines and priorities.

Of course, the logical time used to express environment constraints must eventually be reconciled with the physical time on the platform. Platform timing constraints must take into account performance issues, such as worst-case execution times (WCETs) and processor utilization. Here, the actual computation times of the different software components are more important than their relative speeds in order to determine their schedulability on the chosen platform.

Our proposal for a multirate synchronous implementation of IEC 61499 shifts the burden of reconciling environment time with platform time from the programmer to the toolchain. The programmer simply specifies the relative execution periods of different resources for a given IEC 61499 system. These periods are given as an integral multiple of a user-defined base period. So, for example, if the base period is defined to be 10ms, then three resources with the relative periods of 1, 5, and 10 would be executed once every 10ms, 50ms, and 100ms, respectively. This essentially provides a means to automatically check if the ideal assumptions of synchronous reactions can be fulfilled on a given platform using a particular schedule.

In order to reconcile environment time with platform time, a multi-task multirate synchronous program is, first, generated using our compiler from an IEC 61499 specification. Then, static timing analysis is performed for each generated task, as well as for relevant RTOS services to ensure that the taskset remains schedulable even for the worst-case execution times on the chosen platform. The schedulability test is done assuming the rate-monotonic scheduling policy. These steps provide a rigorous and verifiable approach for designing realtime applications with IEC 61499. Since a resource in IEC 61499 is a functional unit of software that has its own execution schedule [5], it provides a natural boundary for splitting an IEC 61499 application into separate synchronous tasks. Function blocks that are connected in a network within a resource are viewed as running synchronously in parallel with each other [10]. In the proposed solution, we have created a new resource type, called MR RESOURCE (short for multirate resource), to facilitate this mapping into synchronous tasks. MR RESOURCE has two parameters that may be customized by the programmer. The first parameter is the period, which allows the programmer to specify the relative periods of each resource as described above. The second parameter is the priority. It is used to specify execution precedence only for resources with the same periods, since rate-monotonic scheduling will already assign priorities in reverse period-duration order (i.e., resources with the shortest period will be given the highest priority).

Once all the resources have been mapped into separate tasks and the relevant WCETs obtained, their schedulability on the target platform must be checked to ensure that the multitask implementation preserves the semantics of the original multirate synchronous model. This schedulability criterion is given in the following subsection.

div.head: A. Static-priority pre-emptive scheduling
div.p: A key challenge in deriving concrete implementations of synchronous programs lies in ensuring behavioural and temporal equivalence with the original model. For a singletask implementation, this equivalence is maintained by simply ensuring that

This inequality is the criterion to correctly reconcile the environment's timing constraint with the platform's timing constraint: A task will remain reactive so long as each of its reactions completes within one period interval of the real-time clock driving that task.

This criterion can be extended to multi-task, multirate programs by considering a set of tasks, P = {p 1 , p 2 , p 3 , ...}, and their corresponding periods, Π = {π(α 1 ), π(α 2 ), π(α 3 ), ...}. As an example, consider a scenario where there are three tasks, p 1 , p 2 , p 3 , with a period of 4ms, 8ms, and 20ms, respectively, and π(α b ) was initially chosen to be 1ms. In this case, τ b = gcd(4, 8, 20) = 4. Then, from equation 2, the largest base period that can be used to satisfy the timing constraints of the task-set is 4ms.

For our purpose, we make use of rate-monotonic scheduling (RMS) [13], which is a static-priority pre-emptive scheduling policy. In RMS, tasks with shorter periods are assigned higher priorities. We assume that no two tasks have the same priority, that is, for tasks with equal periods, we expect their relative priorities to be specified. This implies a deterministic scheduling policy, meaning that at any given time, there is a unique task that may be executed and, hence, a unique behaviour to be expected. div.p: The other i term in inequalities 3 and 4 accounts for the scheduler overheads, such as the context-switching time between tasks. The multiplication with the ceiling'ed quotient in (4) ensures that there will be sufficient time to schedule the higher priority tasks multiple times before scheduling any of the lower priority ones. This time budget is necessary, since for all tasks other than p 1 , the time budget must be sufficient to allow for each task to be interrupted by its predecessors.

To illustrate this, suppose we have three tasks, p 1 , p 2 , p 3 , with the respective periods of 4ms, 8ms, and 20ms, as before. Let W CET (p i )+other i , i ∈ {1, 2, 3}, be 1ms, 3ms, and 7ms, respectively for each task. Task p 1 is clearly schedulable, as inequality 3 can be easily verified. In order to ensure that p 2 is schedulable, inequality 4 needs to be satisfied. Substituting with appropriate values, inequality 4 becomes (2×1ms)+3ms < 8ms, and, hence, p 2 is also schedulable. The substitution shows that sufficient slack time exists in the timing constraint to allow for p 1 to be scheduled twice during p 2 's period. When this substitution is repeated for task p 3 , inequality 4 becomes (5×1ms)+(3×3ms)+7ms < 20ms. This time, the inequality is not satisfied and p 3 cannot be admitted into the schedulable task-set.

Meeting these scheduling constraints and ensuring that the scheduler is deterministic, however, are insufficient to ensure the overall determinism of multirate programs in a multitasking environment. There are two other factors that need to be considered:

1) Task pre-emptions may result in data corruptions during communication. A task writing to (reading from) a buffer may be pre-empted before it finishes writing (reading), leaving the data in an inconsistent state. This can be avoided by ensuring atomic read and write operations. 2) Variations in execution times of tasks may result in out-of-order read and write operations. Read operations may get delayed if reader tasks are pre-empted, while write operations may happen too soon if writer tasks complete their executions very quickly.
We will illustrate some of the problems that arise, and describe our solution for them in the next section.

div.head: IV. INTERTASK COMMUNICATION IN MULTIRATE PROGRAMS
div.p: When considering communication among tasks with multiple execution rates, three scenarios are possible:

div.head: 1) communication between slow and fast tasks;
div.p: 2) communication between fast and slow tasks; and 3) communication between tasks of the same rate.
We discuss these three scenarios in the following subsections.

div.head: A. Slow-to-fast task communication
div.p: Consider, as a first example, the communication scenario depicted in Fig. 2. It consists of two tasks, p 1 and p 2 , with p 1 running at twice the rate of p 2 . Data exchange between each pair of communicating tasks takes place via a unit size buffer. The incoming and outgoing arrows indicate data being written to, and read out from, the buffer, respectively.

In each of its cycle, p 2 completes its reaction shortly before the start of its next cycle, at which point, it writes to the buffer. Task p 1 pre-empts p 2 in each of those cycles, as indicated by the broken bars of p 2 in the figure. At the start of the (j +2)th cycle (coincident with the (k+1)th cycle), p 1 begins execution and reads from the buffer the data that was written there by p 2 in the kth cycle. At the start of the (j + 3)th cycle (midway through the (k + 1)th cycle), p 1 gets executed once more and, again, reads from the buffer. Since p 2 has not completed its computation for the (k + 1)th cycle, the data that p 1 reads is still that produced by p 2 in the kth cycle. Thus, task p 1 can be thought of as having oversampled the data produced by p 2 in the previous (kth) cycle. Without this unit delay, the values read by p 1 maybe unpredictable, as the contents in buffer may have only been partially modified by p 2 . The use of a unit delay is the only non-blocking solution to this problem. Other approaches to ensure that p 1 will only read predictable values require the use of some form of mutex between p 1 and p 2 , which would result in a blocking solution. Since non-blocking implementations are generally easier, our solution requires that slow-to-fast task communication take place only after a one-cycle delay of the slow task. Sometimes, it may be possible that a slow task completes its reaction in a much shorter time than its period. Fig. 3 shows an example of this, where p 2 completes during the jth cycle of p 1 . While p 2 is now able to write to the buffer before the start of p 1 's (j +1)th cycle, the write operation is postponed to the end of p 2 's period, as indicated by the arrow in the figure. Task p 1 would still read from the buffer only in the (j + 2)th cycle, i.e., after a unit delay of p 2 's clock. This consistency of one clock cycle delay is necessary to ensure deterministic data access, irrespective of the execution time of a task. Thus, in order to ensure consistent behaviour, a fast task should always oversample the data produced by a slow task after a one-cycle delay of the slow task's clock. This is a sufficient condition that will always hold due to the following: 1) A fast task can always oversample data produced by a slow task because RMS ensures that a fast task has higher priority and can, therefore, preempt a slow task to sample data at higher rate than the update rate. 2) A one-cycle delay of a slow task's clock is unambiguous, since all task periods are integral multiples of a common base period.

div.head: B. Fast-to-slow task communication
div.p: In contrast to the slow-to-fast task communication, which requires a unit delay to ensure data consistency, communication from a fast task to a slow task may occur immediately after the completion of the fast task's cycle. However, a fast task should not communicate with a slow task while the slow task is computing its reaction. This restriction is necessary to ensure that the data operated on by the slow task will not be externally modified midway through the reaction.

We illustrate this using Fig. 4, which shows the timing diagram for the communication taking place between two tasks, p 1 and p 2 , where p 1 is running at twice the rate of p 2 . In the jth cycle, p 1 sends data to p 2 via a buffer at the end of its reaction. This is immediately read by p 2 , which is starting its kth cycle. In the (j + 1)th cycle, p 1 again writes to the buffer at the end of its reaction. However, as p 2 has yet to complete its reaction for the kth cycle, it refrains from sampling the contents in the buffer just yet. Due to p 2 's slower rate, p 2 effectively undersamples the data produced by p 1 . This ensures that the values read by p 2 at the start of its reaction remains consistent for the entire duration of its period, with all other incoming data ignored until then. This sampling at the start of each new cycle of a slow task must be adhered to even in the presence of other tasks with intermediary rates-tasks with intermediate priorities should never be allowed to hold up a sampling operation. Consider, for example, the scenario in Fig. 5, which shows three tasks, p 1 , Fig. 6. Timing diagram showing bi-directional communication between two tasks running at the same rate, with a unit delay in one direction. p 2 , and p 3 , with relative periods 1 , τ 2 = 2τ 1 , and τ 3 = 4τ 1 , respectively. The start of p 3 's execution is delayed by p 2 , which has higher priority. Despite this delay, the data from p 1 which p 3 samples still needs to be correctly maintained, so that it will always have a consistent view of its environment. This is accomplished by having p 1 communicate with p 2 and p 3 via separate buffers. Fig. 5 shows p 1 writing to both buffers in its jth cycle. In the (j + 1)th cycle, p 1 again writes to Buffer1, but it is disallowed from writing to Buffer2, as indicated by the crossed out arrow. At this point, p 3 has yet to begin its execution for the mth cycle and, hence, the data in Buffer2

should not yet be overwritten. The data in Buffer2 should only be updated once it has been read by p 3 . Thus, in summary, a slow task should always sample the data produced by a fast task at the start of each slow cycle, and hold this value constant for the entire duration of its period. This is a sufficient condition to ensure consistent behaviour. It will always hold due to the following: 1) Data exchange between each pair of communicating tasks takes place via a dedicated unit size buffer. 2) A buffer will only be updated if it is empty (previously written data has already been read), or if one period of the receiving task has elapsed since the buffer was last written to.

div.head: C. Communication among tasks of the same rate
div.p: Communication between tasks running at the same rate does not pose any particular challenge, unlike that of the former two scenarios. However, for tasks that communicate each to the other, such that a communication cycle is formed between them, we require the cycle be broken by a unit delay, i.e., instantaneous communication cycles are not allowed. This is necessary as compositions of synchronous tasks with instantaneous communication cycles may not always have finite reactions [9]. Consider, for example, two tasks, p 1 and p 2 , that communicate each to the other, as shown in Fig. 6. Task p 1 sends data, which is read by p 2 in the same cycle; however, data sent by p 2 is read by p 1 only in the next cycle. This systematic use of a unit delay to prevent instantaneous communication cycles provides a simple way to ensure finite reactions in compositions of synchronous tasks.

div.head: V. IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: For prototyping purposes, we extended the function block compiler, FBC [17], [18], with the capability to generate multi-task code for the μC/OS-II RTOS. FBC was originally developed to synthesize single-rate synchronous and GALS programs from IEC 61499 descriptions. Unlike other code generators for IEC 61499 (e.g., FBDK [6] and 4DIAC-IDE [7]), the code produced by FBC can be executed without the need of any run-time environment. This provided a suitable starting point for our extensions, as no consideration needed to be given to the characteristics of any run-time environment. The extensions to FBC include the following: 1) A new set of communication function block templates to implement the multirate communication patterns.
2) The ability to generate multi-task, multirate synchronous programs utilizing μC/OS-II services.
3) The ability to generate annotated code for the static timing analyser described in [19].
These aspects are described in the following subsections.

div.head: A. Communication function blocks
div.p: In IEC 61499, communication function blocks are used to describe various communication patterns between resources. Specific communication properties may be described, while hiding the underlying mechanisms from the application. Fig. 7 shows a pair of send and receive communication function blocks for communication between resources of different rates. These blocks have been named as SENDuCOS n and RECVuCOS n, where n is a non-negative integer denoting the number of data elements to be sent/received. For example, a value of n = 2 would be used to describe a SENDuCOS and RECVuCOS pair with input ports SD 1 and SD 2, and output ports RD 1 and RD 2, respectively.

Data that is to be sent to another resource should be connected to the SD n input ports of the SENDuCOS block. Then, whenever the REQ input event is received, data from the SD n input ports will be conditionally written to a shared buffer, as described in the preceding section. Meanwhile, the CNF event will be emitted as confirmation that data has been written, and may be used to trigger other function blocks.

The ID input port provides a means to pair a SENDuCOS block with a RECVuCOS block by assigning a unique name to each pair. This pairing must be a one-to-one association between a SENDuCOS and a RECVuCOS block. An example of this pairing is depicted in Fig. 1 by the actualSpeed blocks in the ShaftTask and ControllerTask resources. In the RECVuCOS block, data will be retrieved from the shared buffer and placed on the RD n output port. The IND output event will be emitted whenever there is meaningful data to be read. Internally, these blocks implement the delayed and sampling operations, as described previously. During compilation, both the send and receive blocks get compiled into code that runs at the rate of the resource in which they reside. The generated code always maintains the following discipline: 1) Reads from the shared buffer occur only at the beginning of a resource's period. 2) Reads/writes to/from the shared buffer momentarily disables the μC/OS-II scheduler to ensure the atomicity of such operations.
The description of the SENDuCOS/RECVuCOS blocks is elaborated in Section V-B, when we discuss the nature of the multitask code generated.

div.head: B. Multi-task code generation
div.p: The process of generating multirate programs in FBC begins by giving it as input a set of IEC 61499 resources that is to be executed on a given device. FBC will do a depth-first traversal of the network in each of the resource, recursively entering each composite block it encounters, to perform a bottom-up compilation of the network. The resulting output from FBC is C code, with each resource mapped to a corresponding μC/OS-II task. A top-level file that sets up all tasks with their appropriate priorities and starts the RTOS is also generated. We focus here on the generation of multitasking code from resources, and refer the reader to [17], [18] for details on the code generation process for the basic, composite, and service interface function blocks.

Every synchronous task will run at its own rate within μC/OS-II. Each task, with the relative period of τ i , will have the standard code structure as shown in Fig. 8. The actual physical time is noted at the start of each logical time instant (line 2). Then, the C functions that implement the behaviour of each function block in the network will be called, starting with the RECVuCOS blocks (lines 3-4).

Whenever the SENDuCOS block is used to send data from a slow resource to a fast resource, it ensures that writes to the shared buffer only takes place at the end of the slow resource's period, i.e., in the last τ b interval of the slow resource's period. Consequently, data from slow to fast resources will not be prematurely written to the buffer, as illustrated earlier in Fig. 3.

In our implementation, this is achieved by rescheduling the invocation of the SENDuCOS block in the task of the slow resource whenever it finishes early, rather than by an explicit delay within the SENDuCOS block itself. This has the advantage of making the code of the SENDuCOS block re-entrant to other tasks. SENDuCOS blocks that need to be rescheduled are noted accordingly, while the actual reschedule operation is performed within the task itself (lines 5-14). The rescheduling is done by computing the remaining slack time of the task (lines 6-7). If the slack time is greater than the base period, the task will be momentarily suspended to ensure that the rescheduled send operations will only take place in the last τ b interval of the task's period. Otherwise, the rescheduled send operations will be performed immediately. In any case, once all computations and communication have been performed for a given clock cycle of the task, the final remaining slack time will be computed, and the task will be appropriately suspended depending on its given period (lines [15][16][17].

When data is being sent from a fast resource to a slow resource, data may be written to the shared buffer at a rate that is faster than that of the slow resource. However, since the RECVuCOS block in the slow resource will only read from the shared buffer at the beginning of its period (our first axiom), the undersampling rule is still adhered to. For the case where the slow resource's period, τ r is an integral multiple of the fast resource's period, τ s , the SENDuCOS block simply writes to the shared buffer whenever the contents of the buffer has been retrieved by the corresponding RECVuCOS block. However, if the resource periods are not integral multiples of each other, the SENDuCOS block will write to the shared buffer whenever the buffer contents have been retrieved, as well as whenever an update is required due to the sampling rate.

In the RECVuCOS block, data will be retrieved from the shared buffer whenever new contents are available at the start of each new period of its containing task. This is possible, since the correct contents of the buffer at each clock boundary would have been ensured by the SENDuCOS block. If the RECVuCOS block is retrieving data written by a slow resource, then the previous value returned to RD n will be reused until a new value is received, adhering to the oversampling requirement.

div.head: C. WCET analysis and results
div.p: To test the practicality of our approach, FBC was used to generate multitasking code for the cruise control and monitoring system introduced in Section II. The full system consists of 18 function block instances, which resulted in 2,460 lines of C code. This includes all necessary auxiliary code required to compile and link against μC/OS-II libraries, but does not include any μC/OS-II source or header file.

Our evaluation platform was the MicroBlaze soft-core processor from Xilinx [20]. The processor was configured with a three-stage pipeline, and with the branch delay slot enabled. The whole program fitted onto the available on-chip memory. Hence, we did not need to consider variances in cache and main memory access times in our timing analysis. The code generated by FBC only makes direct calls to seven μC/OS-II services, three of which are called only at program start-up. Thus, the cost of these functions are of little interest to us, as they do not affect the schedulability of tasks. The cost of the remaining functions, OSTimeGet(), OSTimeDly(), OSSchedLock(), and OSSchedUnLock(), however, need to be accounted for, as they are used to adjust task release times, and to ensure atomic access to shared buffers.

The invocation of OSTimeDly() and OSSchedUnLock() may cause μC/OS-II's scheduler to be called, resulting in a possible context-switch. Also, the occurrence of interrupts may cause scheduling and context-switching to take place. The execution time of μC/OS-II's scheduler interrupt is directly proportional to the number of tasks created, but the scheduling time is constant regardless of the number of tasks [14]. This, however, is not problematic, since the number of tasks is known beforehand, and will not change during run-time. The code that performs context-switching, as well as enabling and disabling of interrupts, consists mainly of single-path functions. They are easily analysed and their execution times can be approximated as constants.

For each task, FBC generates annotated code for the timing analyser described in [19]. The annotation bounds the enclosing loop of each task (refer to Fig. 8) to one iteration, and marks the end of the loop with a special tag to indicate the end of a synchronous reaction. Each pass of the loop corresponds to a single reaction of the synchronous task.

For each WCET value computed by the timing analyser, the timing analyser is able to record the path taken to obtain the WCET. By manually setting the appropriate variables in the program, we were able to measure the actual execution time taken for each of the longest paths reported by the timing analyser. The results of the WCET returned by the timing analyser, as well as from our measurements, are shown in Table I. On average, the percentage of overestimation is 15 percent. This amount is modest, and should not be prohibitive in practical safety-critical applications.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: Much work has already been done in the area of automatic code generation from high-level models, with tools such as SIMULINK [3] and SCADE [4], being prominent examples. They have traditionally been used to generate single-task programs, but proposals to derive multitasking, multirate code have also been made. The work in [21] derives multirate software on several tasks from the code obtained from SCADE. However, that work mostly discussed issues regarding the implementation of bi-rate programs and did not present any means to do this automatically. The programmer is responsible for manually integrating the single-task code obtained from SCADE to create a multi-task, multirate program.

Efforts to derive multi-task multirate code from SIMULINK appeared in [22] and [23]. In [22], SIMULINK blocks were given a synchronous reactive (SR) semantics. Then, two task communication mechanisms for one-to-one communication and for single-writer multiple-reader scenarios were presented. Efficient buffer usage was an important consideration in this work. On the other hand, [23] translated SIMULINK into LUSTRE++, which is LUSTRE code [24] with meta-operators for representing common RTOS features. The tools described in [22] and [23] generated multi-task code for the OSEK OS [25] standard and the Xenomai RTOS [26], respectively.

The rate transition blocks [27] in SIMULINK also shares similarity with the work here. Rate transition blocks enable communication between blocks operating at different rates, with various parameters to trade data integrity and deterministic transfer for faster response or lower memory requirements. The SENDuCOS and RECVuCOS function blocks are much simpler, and resemble rate transition blocks that have been set to ensure data integrity and deterministic data transfer.

Related work also appeared in [2], [28], which dealt primarily with multi-task implementations of synchronous programs using memory-optimal communication buffers. It did not target any specific modelling language or RTOS, but focus more on semantic preservation under different scheduling polices. The technique of oversampling and undersampling data to facilitate communication from slow and fast tasks, respectively, had been similarly applied there. This is a common approach used to bridge communicating tasks of different frequencies, as it is both simple and deterministic. The more recent work of [29] used bounded buffers to avoid data losses due to undersampling, but that has come at the cost of higher memory requirements and implementation complexity.

In the area of WCET analysis, static timing analysis of stand-alone synchronous programs have been demonstrated in [19], [30], [31], while the WCET of most of μC/OS-II's services have been reported in [32] using static techniques that are combined with a lot of manual intervention. We, on the other hand, have adapted the timing analyser in [19] to obtain the WCET for synchronous tasks, as well as a small subset of μC/OS-II's services that are relevant to our work.

To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first attempt to achieve real-time behaviour of IEC 61499 descriptions within a formal multirate synchronous framework. Research on real-time execution of IEC 61499 applications have, so far, been concerned with the mapping of function blocks in a network to real-time tasks [33], [34]. Formal frameworks that ensure timely and deterministic communication between tasks have received far less attention. Also, those works did not provide any means to ensure that function blocks, once mapped to tasks, would be able to meet their timing constraints.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS AND OUTLOOK
div.p: This paper has presented an approach to derive multirate synchronous programs from IEC 61499 descriptions. The multirate programs can be automatically synthesized as multitasking code for the μC/OS-II RTOS, without any further glue code needed to be written by the programmer. This work has also presented a new way to achieve predictable and real-time behaviour from IEC 61499 descriptions. Timing requirements can be given as resource periods using ideal logical time, while the actual execution time be checked using a simple schedulability criterion. The synchronous nature of the generated code, as well as the restricted use of RTOS primitives, make it amenable to static analysis techniques for estimating WCET.

With the advent of many industrial control systems requiring functional safety, this should remain a promising area for future research.
